title: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
summary: How DeepSeekMoE and DeepSeek-V3 route tokens: many small experts, shared experts and bias-based balancing, then building the layer yourself and running MoE across GPUs.
outcomes: Explain how an MoE layer separates total parameters from per-token compute, and compute both for a real config
Explain how the router learns through its gate values, and why an expert it never selects gets no useful gradient
Explain why splitting experts into mN smaller ones and activating mK keeps FLOPs fixed but adds flexibility
Weigh the evidence for and against shared experts across DeepSeek, OLMoE and Qwen3
Compute the auxiliary balance loss and router z-loss, and explain interference gradients and global-batch counting
Trace the bias update of aux-loss-free balancing and DeepSeek-V3's group-limited gate step by step
Implement an MoE layer with sort-based dispatch, index_add_ combine and bias balancing, and test it against a dense MLP
Estimate all-to-all traffic and expert GEMM arithmetic intensity, and explain why MoE decoding is memory-bound

lessons.title: From one MLP to many routed experts

blocks.md: In the GPT you built, every block has an attention layer followed by an MLP (also called the feed-forward network, FFN), and every token goes through all of the MLP's weights. In GPT-2 small, for example, the MLP widens each 768-number vector to an **intermediate width** of 3072 and projects it back to 768, so its two weight matrices hold 2 x 768 x 3072 weights and every token multiplies through all of them. A model like this, where every token uses every weight, is called **dense**. That couples two things you might want to separate: the number of parameters (how much the model can store) and the compute spent per token. Make the MLP 4 times wider and every token pays 4 times the MLP FLOPs.

A **Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layer** (Shazeer et al., 2017) breaks that coupling. It replaces one MLP with $N$ **experts**, each an ordinary MLP with its own weights, plus a small **router** (or gate) that looks at each token and picks only $K$ of the experts to run. Parameters grow with $N$; compute per token grows only with $K$. Two well-known Google MoE Transformers set $K$ differently: **GShard** (Lepikhin et al., 2020) uses $K=2$, and **Switch Transformer** (Fedus, Zoph and Shazeer, 2021) uses $K=1$, switching each token to a single expert. This course follows **DeepSeekMoE** (Dai et al., 2024), an MoE design paper from the lab DeepSeek-AI, and **DeepSeek-V3** (2024), their large model built on it; the formulas use DeepSeekMoE's notation.

The router is just a learned vector per expert, called the expert's **centroid** $e_i$, because it acts like a center point in the space of hidden states: tokens whose vectors point the same way as $e_i$ get a large dot product with it. For the token's **hidden state** $u_t$ (the vector that represents token $t$ when it reaches this layer, after the attention sublayer), it computes an **affinity** score $s_{i,t}$ for every expert (a softmax over the dot products $u_t^\top e_i$), keeps the $K$ largest, and uses them as **gate values** $g_{i,t}$ that weight each chosen expert's output. The softmax turns the $N$ dot products into positive scores that sum to 1, so each score reads as how strongly the router prefers that expert. Experts that are not chosen get gate 0 and are never computed.

blocks.tex: h_t = u_t + \sum_{i=1}^{N} g_{i,t}\,\mathrm{FFN}_i(u_t),\qquad g_{i,t} = \begin{cases} s_{i,t} & s_{i,t} \in \mathrm{Topk}(\{s_{j,t}\}, K) \\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases},\qquad s_{i,t} = \mathrm{Softmax}_i(u_t^\top e_i)
blocks.caption: The conventional MoE layer from the DeepSeekMoE paper (layer norm omitted). In words: the output is the input $u_t$ plus each expert's output times its gate, and a gate is the expert's score if that score is among the $K$ largest, otherwise 0.

blocks.title: Router affinities for 4 tokens and 4 experts, top-2

scenes.caption: Each row is one token's softmax over the 4 experts, so each row sums to 1. These are toy numbers computed from made-up logits; a real router produces them from $u_t^\top e_i$.
Token t1 keeps its two largest scores: E1 (0.61) and E3 (0.22). Its MoE output is $u + 0.61\,\mathrm{FFN}_1(u) + 0.22\,\mathrm{FFN}_3(u)$. E2 and E4 are never run for this token.
Every token picks its own pair: t2 uses E2 and E4, t3 uses E1 and E2, t4 uses E3 and E4. Only half of the expert weights run for each token.

Count the picks per column: each expert received 2 of the 8 slots (4 tokens x top-2 picks). This batch happens to be perfectly balanced. Nothing in the routing rule guarantees that, which is the problem of lessons 4 and 5.

blocks.title: One MoE layer: route, run K experts, combine

scenes.caption: The MoE layer sits where the MLP used to be. The router scores all experts, but only the chosen ones do any matrix multiplies.
Token t1: the router picks E1 and E3. Their outputs are scaled by the gate values 0.61 and 0.22 and summed with the residual.
Token t4 takes a different path through the same layer: E3 (0.72) and E4 (0.12). Different tokens use different parameters, which is how total parameters exceed per-token compute.

blocks.md: How does the router learn, if picking the top $K$ is a hard yes-or-no choice? Through the gates. A chosen expert's output is multiplied by its gate $g_{i,t} = s_{i,t}$, so the loss depends smoothly on that score. By the chain rule, $\partial \mathcal{L} / \partial s_{i,t} = (\partial \mathcal{L} / \partial h_t) \cdot \mathrm{FFN}_i(u_t)$: the gradient arriving at the layer's output, dotted with what expert $i$ produced. If the expert's output points the way that lowers the loss, this is negative, so gradient descent raises the score, and the gradient flows on into the logit $u_t^\top e_i$ and the centroid $e_i$. The top-K step itself has no gradient: it only decides which experts are in the sum.

A worked example: 4 experts, top-2. Logits $(2.0, 0.5, 1.2, -0.3)$ give softmax scores $(0.564, 0.126, 0.253, 0.057)$, so E1 and E3 run. Say the dot products $(\partial \mathcal{L}/\partial h) \cdot \mathrm{FFN}_i(u)$ come out as $-0.8$ for E1 (its output helps) and $+0.5$ for E3 (its output hurts). Backpropagating through the gates and the softmax (computed with PyTorch autograd) gives the logit gradients in the figure. E2 and E4 still get a small gradient, but only through the softmax's shared denominator, so its size depends on how E1 and E3 did, never on what E2 or E4 would have computed.

blocks.title: Router gradient for one token: only the chosen experts are judged

scenes.caption: Softmax scores. Top-2 keeps E1 (0.564) and E3 (0.253); their outputs are computed and weighted by these gates.
Gradient of the loss with respect to each logit: E1 -0.268 (descent raises it), E3 +0.209 (descent lowers it). E2 +0.041 and E4 +0.018 come only from the softmax denominator.
Suppose E4 would have helped even more than E1 (a dot product of -0.6). Its gradient is still +0.018: the router is never told, because E4's output was never computed.

blocks.md: A router only learns about the experts it actually runs. An expert that is never selected never produces an output, so no gradient ever says it would have helped; with a softmax its logit only moves through the shared denominator, and that push is downward whenever the chosen experts helped. With a per-expert sigmoid (lesson 6) an unchosen expert gets exactly zero gradient. This is the mechanism behind the collapse in the question below.

Separate two numbers for every MoE model: **total parameters** (all experts, what you store) and **activated parameters** (what one token actually uses, which sets FLOPs per token). DeepSeek-V3 has 671B total and 37B activated per token.

This course is about three refinements DeepSeek-AI introduced on top of this layer: **fine-grained experts** (many small experts instead of a few big ones), **shared experts** (a few experts that every token uses), and **auxiliary-loss-free load balancing** (keeping experts evenly used without adding a balancing term to the loss). DeepSeek-V3 combines all three.

blocks.question: An MoE layer has 16 experts, each the same size as the dense MLP it replaced, with top-2 routing. Compared with the dense MLP, what happens to parameters and per-token FLOPs in that layer?
options: Both grow 16 times
Parameters grow 2 times; FLOPs grow 16 times
Parameters grow 16 times; per-token FLOPs grow about 2 times, plus a tiny router cost
Parameters grow 16 times; per-token FLOPs stay exactly the same as dense
blocks.explain: Every expert is stored, so parameters scale with N = 16. Each token runs only K = 2 experts, so expert FLOPs are 2 times the dense MLP. The router (one dot product per expert) adds a little on top. With top-1 routing (Switch), expert FLOPs would match the dense MLP.

blocks.question: A router scores experts with a sigmoid per expert, $s_i = \sigma(u^\top e_i)$, and top-2 picks E1 and E3 for a token. What gradient does this token send to E2's centroid $e_2$?
options: A gradient proportional to how much E2 would have lowered the loss
Exactly zero: $s_2$ appears nowhere in the layer's output, and the top-K choice has no gradient
The same gradient as E1, because all experts share the router
A negative gradient, because unchosen experts are always penalized
blocks.explain: With a sigmoid, each score depends only on its own logit, and only the chosen experts' scores multiply an output. E2's output was never computed, so nothing in the loss depends on $s_2$. With a softmax, E2 would get a small gradient through the shared denominator, but still not one that measures E2's own usefulness.

blocks.prompt: In the figure, all four experts got exactly 2 token slots. Will a learned router keep load balanced like this on its own as training goes on?
blocks.reveal: Not reliably. Shazeer et al. (2017) observed that the gating network (their name for the router) tends to converge to always giving large weights to the same few experts, and that this is self-reinforcing: favored experts train faster, so they get picked even more. This is **routing collapse**, and every method in lessons 4 to 6 exists to prevent it.

lessons.title: Fine-grained experts: split each expert into m slices

blocks.md: Conventional MoE models use a small number of experts, for example 8 or 16. The DeepSeekMoE paper argues this causes **knowledge hybridity**: with so few experts, the tokens routed to any one expert cover many unrelated kinds of knowledge, so that expert must cram them all into one set of weights that are hard to use at the same time.

**Fine-grained expert segmentation** fixes this without changing the budget. Take each expert's MLP and cut its intermediate width (the inner layer, 3072 in GPT-2 small) into $m$ slices, giving $mN$ experts that are each $1/m$ the size. Each slice keeps its share of the first matrix's output columns and the matching rows of the second matrix, so it is a complete small MLP with $1/m$ of the weights, and running all $m$ slices costs what one full expert did. To keep compute constant, activate $mK$ of them instead of $K$. Total expert parameters stay at $N$ standard MLPs, and per-token FLOPs stay at $K$ standard MLPs.

blocks.title: The same 16 hidden units, cut ever finer

scenes.caption: Conventional: 4 experts (N = 4), each 4 hidden units wide, top-1 routing (K = 1). One token can only use one fixed block of 4 units.
m = 2: 8 experts of 2 units each, top-2. Still 4 active units per token, same FLOPs, but the token can now take half of the old E1 and half of the old E4.
m = 4: 16 experts of 1 unit each, top-4. Same 16 parameters' worth of units, same 4 active per token, but any 4 of 16 can be combined. This is the mN choose mK flexibility the paper is after.

blocks.tex: h_t = u_t + \sum_{i=1}^{mN} g_{i,t}\,\mathrm{FFN}_i(u_t),\qquad g_{i,t} \neq 0 \ \text{only for}\ s_{i,t} \in \mathrm{Topk}(\{s_{j,t}\}_{j=1}^{mN},\ mK)
blocks.caption: Fine-grained MoE: same equation as before with $mN$ experts and $mK$ active. Each $\mathrm{FFN}_i$ now has $1/m$ of the original intermediate width.

blocks.md: The gain is in the number of distinct expert combinations a token can use. The count is $\binom{n}{k}$, read n choose k: the number of ways to pick $k$ of $n$ items when order does not matter, n factorial divided by k factorial and by (n minus k) factorial. With $N = 16$ and top-2 there are $\binom{16}{2} = 16 \times 15 / 2 = 120$ combinations. Split each expert in 4 ($m = 4$) and activate 8 of 64: $\binom{64}{8} = 4{,}426{,}165{,}368$. The parameter count and FLOPs did not change; only the menu got far richer.

blocks.title: Possible expert combinations per token (log10), N = 16, K = 2

scenes.caption: Conventional top-2 of 16 experts gives 120 combinations, about $10^{2.08}$.
Splitting each expert further keeps FLOPs fixed, yet the count of combinations explodes: m = 4 gives about 4.4 billion, and m = 8 about $10^{20}$.

blocks.md: Does it work? The paper scores models by **Pile test loss**: the average next-token cross-entropy (the loss you trained GPT with) on held-out text from **the Pile** (Gao et al., 2020), an 825 GiB public English corpus that EleutherAI assembled from 22 sources such as web pages, books, arXiv papers and GitHub code. Lower means better prediction. In the paper's 2B-parameter validation runs (100B training tokens, all MoE models with the same total parameters), the Pile test loss fell from 1.867 for GShard (top-2) to 1.808 for DeepSeekMoE with the same activated parameters. DeepSeekMoE here is fine-grained and also uses one shared expert, the topic of the next lesson. It matched a GShard model with 1.5 times the expert parameters and compute (also 1.808). The figure also includes **Hash Layer** (Roller et al., 2021), which sends each token to an expert by a fixed hash of its token id instead of a learned router.

blocks.title: Pile test loss, 2B-scale MoE comparisons (lower is better)

scenes.caption: Dense is the 0.2B baseline. Hash Layer and Switch (top-1) have 0.2B active; GShard (top-2) and DeepSeekMoE have 0.3B active; all MoE models have 2.0B total. Numbers from DeepSeekMoE Table 1.
GShard x1.5 has 1.5 times the expert parameters and expert compute of GShard, yet only ties DeepSeekMoE at 1.808 (Table 2).

blocks.md: Finer is not free forever. Each expert becomes a smaller matrix multiply, which gives the GPU less work per launch to spread over its many parallel cores, so it runs less efficiently. DeepSeekMoE 16B stopped at experts one quarter the size of a standard FFN, citing the potential loss of computational efficiency from excessively small experts. DeepSeek-V3 uses 256 routed experts with an intermediate width of 2048; lesson 8 works out what that means on a GPU.

The paper's **ablation** (an experiment that changes one design choice and holds everything else fixed; Figure 3) segmented each expert into 2 and then 4 pieces while holding total and activated parameters fixed, and saw overall benchmark performance improve with each step of finer granularity.

A later study turned this into a scaling law. Krajewski et al. (2024), *Scaling Laws for Fine-Grained Mixture of Experts*, define **granularity** $G = d_{ff} / d_{expert}$: the dense model's FFN width divided by one expert's width, the same thing as this lesson's $m$. A token is routed to $G$ times as many experts, so active parameters stay fixed. From over 100 training runs (129M to 3.7B parameters, 16B to 130B tokens, $G$ from 1 to 16, with total expert parameters fixed at 64 times one FFN) they fitted the loss as a function of total non-embedding parameters $N$, training tokens $D$ and $G$:

blocks.tex: L(N, D, G) = c + \left(\frac{g}{G^{\gamma}} + a\right)\frac{1}{N^{\alpha}} + \frac{b}{D^{\beta}},\qquad g = 2.1,\ \gamma = 0.58,\ a = 18.1,\ \alpha = 0.115
blocks.caption: Eq. 9 and Table 1 of Krajewski et al. Raising $G$ shrinks only the $g/G^{\gamma}$ part, so the gain from finer experts flattens out; the constant $a$ is the part of the parameter term that no granularity removes.

blocks.md: Their conclusions: making each expert the size of the dense FFN ($G = 1$) is not optimal at almost any compute budget; the best $G$ grows with the budget; and with $N$, $D$ and $G$ all chosen well, MoE beats a dense Transformer by a margin that widens with scale. Two caveats. Routing work grows with $G$: for a model with 7M active parameters (64 x 7M in total) trained on A100 GPUs, $G = 16$ lost to $G = 8$ in wall-clock time because routing dominated. And OLMoE (Muennighoff et al., 2024) saw diminishing returns: going from 8 experts (1 active) to 32 (4 active) improved HellaSwag and MMLU (multiple-choice questions across 57 subjects) by about 10%, the next step to 64 (8 active) by 1 to 2%. In these terms DeepSeek-V3 has $G = 18432 / 2048 = 9$: its dense FFN is 9 experts wide, and each token runs 9 experts (1 shared and 8 routed).

blocks.title: Compute-optimal granularity rises with the training budget

scenes.caption: Compute-optimal $G$ from the fitted law (Krajewski et al., Table 2, expansion rate 64): 8 at the smallest budget, rising to 16, 32 and 64 as the budget grows.
All of these are predictions of the fitted law: the runs behind it had at most 3.7B total parameters. Read the trend, finer experts for bigger budgets, not the exact values.

blocks.question: You split each of 16 experts into 4 (64 experts total) but forget to change top-2 routing. What happens?
options: Per-token expert compute drops to one quarter, because 2 small experts are only half of one original expert
Nothing changes; the layer has the same parameters and FLOPs
Per-token compute rises 4 times because there are 4 times as many experts
The router stops working because softmax needs exactly 16 outputs
blocks.explain: Segmentation keeps compute constant only if you also raise the number of active experts from K to mK, here from 2 to 8. With top-2 of 64 quarter-size experts, each token uses 2/4 = 0.5 of one original expert instead of 2, a quarter of the FLOPs. Total parameters are unchanged.

blocks.question: Why is the combinatorial count, not the expert count, the quantity the paper highlights?
options: Because more combinations means more FLOPs
Because routers need at least a billion options to converge
Because GPUs schedule experts by combination
Because each token's computation is a sum over its chosen experts, so more possible subsets means a more precisely targeted mix of knowledge at the same cost
blocks.explain: A token's MoE output is the gated sum of its chosen experts. With 120 possible pairs, many different kinds of tokens must share the same pair. With billions of possible 8-subsets of small experts, the token can assemble a closer fit. FLOPs are identical in both designs.

blocks.question: A team trains a small MoE at a modest budget and finds that $G = 16$ trains slower in wall-clock time than $G = 8$, though $G = 16$ has slightly lower loss per step. Which reading fits the scaling-law paper?
options: Granularity never helps; the law is wrong
Per-step loss keeps improving with $G$, but routing and small-matrix overhead grow with $G$, so the wall-clock optimum can sit at a lower $G$, especially for small models
$G = 16$ must have more active parameters
The loss improvement comes from more total parameters
blocks.explain: Finer experts keep active and total parameters fixed, so the per-step gain is real but diminishing. Krajewski et al. saw exactly this: at 64 x 7M, $G = 8$ beat $G = 16$ in wall-clock time because routing cost dominated. Higher $G$ pays off at larger budgets.

lessons.title: Shared experts: an always-on path for common knowledge

blocks.md: The second problem DeepSeekMoE names is **knowledge redundancy**. Tokens sent to different experts often still need the same common knowledge (basic syntax, frequent words). If every expert must learn it on its own, many experts store copies of the same thing and less capacity is left for specialization.

**Shared expert isolation** gives that common knowledge a home. Set aside $K_s$ experts as **shared experts** that every token passes through, with no router involved. To keep compute constant, the router now picks $mK - K_s$ routed experts instead of $mK$. The paper credits the prototype of this idea to Rajbhandari et al. (2022, DeepSpeed-MoE, from the team behind Microsoft's DeepSpeed training library), who arrived at it from an engineering angle.

blocks.tex: h_t = u_t + \sum_{i=1}^{K_s} \mathrm{FFN}_i(u_t) + \sum_{i=K_s+1}^{mN} g_{i,t}\,\mathrm{FFN}_i(u_t),\qquad g_{i,t}\ \text{nonzero for the top}\ (mK - K_s)\ \text{routed experts}
blocks.caption: The full DeepSeekMoE layer. In words: output equals input, plus every shared expert's output at weight 1 (no gate), plus the gated outputs of the routed experts, where only the top $mK - K_s$ routed gates are nonzero.

blocks.title: Shared expert plus routed experts

scenes.caption: The shared expert S has no router edge: every token goes through it. Routed experts R1 to R6 stand in for the many fine-grained experts.
A code token: S runs, and the router adds R1 and R4 for the specialized part.
A math token: S runs again, but the routed pair is now R2 and R6. Common knowledge lives in S once, so the routed experts do not each need a copy.

blocks.md: Evidence from the 2B experiments. Trained from scratch, isolating one shared expert in a GShard-style model improved most benchmarks (Figure 3 of the paper). And in the trained DeepSeekMoE 2B (1 shared expert and 7 of 63 routed experts active, Pile loss 1.808), switching the shared expert off at evaluation and activating one more routed expert instead (same compute) raised the loss to **2.414**. The routed experts cannot stand in for what the shared expert learned.

How many shared experts? Holding 64 total and the active count fixed, 1, 2 and 4 shared experts gave Pile losses of 1.808, 1.806 and 1.811, a small difference. The authors kept a ratio of 1 shared expert to 3 activated routed experts when scaling up.

Real configurations, from the papers and DeepSeek-V3's released config:

- **DeepSeekMoE 2B**: 1 shared + 63 routed experts, each 0.25 of a standard FFN; 1 + 7 active (2 FFNs' worth).
- **DeepSeekMoE 16B**: 2 shared + 64 routed, each 0.25 of a standard FFN; 2 + 6 active. 16.4B total, 2.8B activated, 74.4T vs 183.5T FLOPs per 4K tokens against DeepSeek 7B, DeepSeek-AI's earlier dense model (74.4 / 183.5, or 40.5%).
- **DeepSeek-V3**: 1 shared + 256 routed, intermediate width 2048, 1 + 8 active, in 58 of its 61 layers (the first 3 stay dense).

This is lesson 2's $G = 9$ seen from the other side: 9 active experts of width 2048 make $9 \times 2048 = 18432$ active hidden units, exactly the intermediate width (`inter_dim` 18432) of the 3 dense FFN layers. Per token, each MoE layer costs the same FLOPs as a dense one while storing 257 experts.

To count V3's parameters you need three more facts. Its hidden vectors are 7168 numbers wide (`dim` in the config). Each expert is a **SwiGLU** MLP (Shazeer, 2020), not GPT-2's two-matrix GELU MLP: it projects the input up twice, passes one copy through the Swish function $x \cdot \sigma(x)$, where $\sigma(x) = 1/(1+e^{-x})$ is the **sigmoid**, a smooth step from 0 to 1, and multiplies the two copies elementwise so one acts as a learned gate on the other (GLU stands for gated linear unit). A third matrix projects back down. So one expert holds $3 \times 7168 \times 2048 \approx 44.0$ million weights. Finally, V3's attention is **multi-head latent attention (MLA)**, which compresses the keys and values each token stores into a smaller latent vector to save memory.

blocks.title: Where DeepSeek-V3's parameters live (billions, from config_671B.json)

scenes.caption: Total: each expert is a SwiGLU MLP with three weight matrices, $3 \times 7168 \times 2048 \approx 44.0$M weights. 58 layers x 256 routed experts is about 653.9B, 97% of the computed 671.0B total. Attention (MLA, V3's compressed attention) is 11.4B.

Activated per token: only 8 routed experts per layer run, about 20.4B, while shared experts, attention, embeddings and dense layers are always used. The bars sum to about 37.4B, or 37.6B with router weights, matching the report's 37B.

blocks.md: Simplified accounting: the bars leave out the 0.1B of router weights and small norm vectors (with them the computed total is 671.0B), and the count covers the 61 main layers only. V3 also ships a 14B multi-token prediction module, an extra layer trained to predict one token further ahead, which is not part of the 671B. The released config and the paper agree.

Not every later open MoE agrees. **OLMoE** (Muennighoff et al., 2024, from the Allen Institute for AI) trained two models from scratch with the same active and total parameters and FLOPs: 32 routed experts with 4 active, versus 31 routed with 3 active plus 1 shared. Both trained similarly and the shared version was slightly worse, so OLMoE-1B-7B ships without a shared expert. Their explanation is lesson 2's combinatorics: turning one routed expert into a shared one cuts the combinations per layer from $\binom{32}{4} = 35{,}960$ to $\binom{31}{3} = 4{,}495$, almost 90% fewer. Note that the 2.414 test above is different: it removes the shared expert from a model trained to rely on it.

blocks.title: OLMoE's ablation: what a shared expert costs in combinations

scenes.caption: Same active compute (4 small experts per token) and same total parameters. Without sharing, a token chooses among 35,960 subsets.
Fixing one expert as always-on leaves 4,495 subsets, 87.5% fewer. In OLMoE's runs this lost slightly more than the shared expert gained.

blocks.md:
What some open MoEs chose, from their papers and reports:

- **Mixtral 8x7B** (Mistral AI, 2024): 8 feedforward experts per layer, each a full FFN as in Mistral 7B, top-2, no shared expert (coarse, $G = 1$).
- **DeepSeekMoE 16B and DeepSeek-V3**: fine-grained routed experts plus 2 and 1 shared experts.
- **OLMoE-1B-7B** (2024): 64 experts, 8 active, no shared expert.
- **Qwen3 MoE** (2025, e.g. Qwen3-235B-A22B): 128 experts, 8 active; the report says that unlike Qwen2.5-MoE, Qwen3-MoE excludes shared experts.

The evidence is mixed. Whether a shared expert pays for itself seems to depend on the granularity (how many combinations it costs) and on the balancing method: OLMoE argues that a balance loss which forces equal use is what stops the model from learning its own always-on experts.

blocks.question: In the 2B ablation, removing the shared expert and activating one extra routed expert kept FLOPs equal but raised Pile loss from 1.808 to 2.414. What is the best reading?
options: The routed experts were undertrained, so any extra routed expert would hurt
The shared expert had learned common knowledge that the specialized routed experts do not hold, so it is not interchangeable with a routed one
Shared experts are larger than routed experts, so removing one removes compute
The loss rose because the router softmax had one fewer output
blocks.explain: Both configurations use the same number and size of active experts. The jump shows the shared expert holds something the routed experts never learned because they could rely on it: the common knowledge the design meant to isolate.

blocks.question: A team configures 2 shared + 64 routed quarter-size experts and routes to 8 routed experts, keeping the same 2 shared. Compared with DeepSeekMoE 16B (2 + 6 active), what changed?
options: Nothing; shared experts do not count toward compute
Total parameters rose by 2 experts
Activated expert compute rose from 8 to 10 quarter-experts, i.e. from 2 to 2.5 standard FFNs per token
Only the router cost changed
blocks.explain: Shared experts always run, so they count fully toward activated compute. DeepSeekMoE lowers the routed top-K by $K_s$ to keep compute fixed: 2 + 6 = 8 quarter-size experts = 2 FFNs. Using 2 + 8 means 10 quarters = 2.5 FFNs, 25% more expert FLOPs.

blocks.question: Two teams report opposite results on shared experts: DeepSeekMoE finds them essential, OLMoE finds a shared expert slightly worse than an extra routed one. Which statement is best supported?
options: One of the two experiments must be wrong
Shared experts only help with softmax routers
It is open: the answer depends on granularity, combinations given up and balancing, and the 2.414 result measures a trained model's dependence, not a from-scratch comparison
Shared experts always help but cost more FLOPs
blocks.explain: Both are careful experiments with different designs. OLMoE compared two models trained from scratch at equal compute; DeepSeekMoE's from-scratch ablation was on a coarse GShard-style model, and its 2.414 number comes from disabling the expert after training. Later designs went both ways (V3 kept one; Qwen3 dropped them).

lessons.title: Load imbalance, routing collapse and the auxiliary loss

blocks.md: Load imbalance hurts in two ways. First, **routing collapse**: the router settles on a few favored experts, those train faster and get picked even more, and the rest are barely trained. Second, systems cost: with **expert parallelism** (different experts on different GPUs), the GPU holding the busiest expert sets the time of the whole step while others idle.

Switch Transformer makes the cost concrete. Switch ran on TPUs (Google's AI accelerator chips), whose compiled programs need **static shapes**: every tensor's size fixed before the run. So each expert gets a fixed **expert capacity**: its fair share, tokens per batch divided by number of experts, times a **capacity factor**. Tokens beyond capacity are **dropped**: the expert skips them and they pass to the next layer only through the residual connection. A larger factor drops fewer tokens but wastes compute and memory on **padding**, the reserved slots an expert does not fill.

blocks.title: Toy batch: 8 tokens, 4 experts, top-1 routing

scenes.caption: A collapsing router sends 5 of 8 tokens to E1 and none to E4. Perfect balance would be 2 each.
Capacity factor 1.0: capacity is 8 / 4 x 1.0 = 2 tokens. E1 drops 3 of its 5 tokens, so 3 of 8 tokens skip this layer's FFN entirely.
Capacity factor 1.5: capacity 3, E1 still drops 2 tokens. Factor 2.0 (capacity 4) drops 1. Buying slack fights the symptom while E4 sits idle.
Balanced routing: 2 tokens per expert. Nothing is dropped even at capacity factor 1.0 and every GPU does equal work.

blocks.md: The standard fix (Shazeer et al. 2017; GShard; Switch) is an **auxiliary balance loss** added to the language-modeling loss (the next-token cross-entropy). In the form used by DeepSeekMoE and the loss-free paper, for $N$ experts, top-$K$ routing and $T$ tokens:

blocks.tex: \mathcal{L}_{\text{Bal}} = \alpha \sum_{i=1}^{N} f_i P_i,\qquad f_i = \frac{N}{K T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \mathbb{1}(\text{token } t \text{ selects expert } i),\qquad P_i = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} s_{i,t}
blocks.caption: $f_i$ is the expert's share of routed slots scaled so that perfect balance gives $f_i = 1$; $P_i$ is its average router score. $\alpha$ sets the strength.

blocks.md: Why the factor $N/(KT)$? $T$ tokens each fill $K$ slots, so there are $KT$ slots, and an even split gives every expert $KT/N$ of them. Dividing an expert's count by that fair share gives $f_i$, so $f_i = 1$ means exactly fair and $f_i = 2$ means twice its share. The scores $P_i$ are averages of softmax outputs, so they sum to 1, and at perfect balance $\sum f_i P_i = \sum P_i = 1$.

Work the toy batch. Balanced: $f = (1, 1, 1, 1)$ and, with uniform scores, $P = (0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25)$, so $\sum f_i P_i = 1.0$. Collapsed: counts $(5, 2, 1, 0)$ give $f = (2.5, 1, 0.5, 0)$; with average scores $P = (0.5, 0.25, 0.15, 0.10)$ the sum is $1.25 + 0.25 + 0.075 + 0 = 1.575$. The loss is larger when the experts that get the most tokens also get the most probability.

$f_i$ comes from a hard top-K count and has no gradient: a count is a step function, since nudging a score slightly does not change which experts win, so its derivative is zero. The gradient flows through $P_i$, the average of the router's softmax scores, which reach the router logits and centroids by the same chain rule as in lesson 1 (here the softmax covers all experts, so every expert's score gets a gradient). It pushes down the scores of overloaded experts. The Switch paper notes the loss is minimized under uniform routing.

blocks.title: Balance loss for 2 experts, top-1, as routing skews

scenes.caption: Simplified: each expert's average score equals its token share. Expert 1 gets share x, so $f_1 = 2x$ and $P_1 = x$; the sum is 2 x squared plus 2 times (1 minus x) squared, lowest at x = 0.5, where the loss is exactly $\alpha$.
A smaller $\alpha$ flattens the whole curve: the push toward balance weakens, and so does the gradient it injects into the router. That knob is the whole dilemma.

blocks.md: **The dilemma.** The balance gradient competes with the language-modeling gradient. The loss-free paper (Wang et al., 2024) swept $\alpha$ over 1e-2, 1e-3, 1e-4 and 0: small $\alpha$ led to routing collapse, large $\alpha$ kept load balanced but notably worsened perplexity. Switch used $\alpha = 10^{-2}$; DeepSeekMoE used 0.01 at 2B and only 0.001 at 16B, noting that a larger factor did not improve efficiency in their setup but did hurt quality.

A balance loss is not a free **regularizer** (an extra loss term that nudges the model toward some property). Its gradient changes the router toward balance, not toward predicting the next token. The loss-free paper calls these **interference gradients**, and they are the reason a strong $\alpha$ costs model quality.

DeepSeekMoE also added a **device-level** balance loss: group the experts by the device they live on and balance the groups instead of individual experts, with a small expert-level $\alpha_1$ (just enough to avoid collapse) and a larger device-level $\alpha_2$. Balancing what the hardware actually waits on, rather than every expert, constrains the router less. The paper used it only for DeepSeekMoE 145B (device factor 0.05); the 2B and 16B models kept all experts on one device and skipped it.

A second auxiliary loss targets stability rather than balance. **ST-MoE** (Zoph et al., 2022) found that large sparse models sometimes diverged and traced part of it to the router: its logits can grow large, and in **bfloat16** (a 16-bit float with an 8-bit exponent and only 7 stored mantissa bits, used for speed) large numbers are coarsely rounded. Representable values between 2 and 4 are about 0.016 apart, but between 1024 and 2048 they are 8 apart, and the softmax's exponential amplifies such errors. The **router z-loss** penalizes the squared log-sum-exp of each token's router logits:

blocks.caption: $B$ tokens, $N$ experts, $x^{(i)}$ the router logits of token $i$ (ST-MoE Eq. 5). Log-sum-exp is a smooth maximum of the logits, so this keeps them small without fixing their order.

blocks.md: A toy token with 4 experts: logits $(1, 0.5, 0, -0.5)$ have log-sum-exp 1.787 and z-loss 3.19. The same ranking scaled tenfold, $(10, 5, 0, -5)$, has log-sum-exp 10.007, z-loss 100.1, and a saturated softmax of $(0.993, 0.007, 0.000, 0.000)$. With weight 0.001, ST-MoE's z-loss made 3 of 3 runs stable (the baseline: 4 of 6) with slightly better quality, where tighter update clipping also stabilized training but badly hurt quality. OLMoE re-tested it at the same weight: fewer loss spikes, lower loss and better downstream scores, for about 2% lower throughput. Both used softmax routers.

The second fix is about *where* $f_i$ is counted. Qiu et al. (2025, Alibaba's Qwen team) note that common MoE training frameworks compute $f_i$ and the balance loss inside each **micro-batch** (the slice one GPU processes per forward pass, as in the gradient accumulation loop of the GPT course) and then average. A micro-batch holds only a few sequences, so the loss is almost **sequence-level**: it pushes even an all-code sequence to spread its tokens over every expert. Their fix synchronizes the counts $f_i$ across all micro-batches (one extra communication of an $N$-number vector) and computes the loss on the **global batch**, so only the whole batch must be even.

blocks.title: Toy: balance per micro-batch vs per global batch

scenes.caption: Toy numbers: 4 micro-batches of one 8-token sequence each, 4 experts (columns E1 to E4), top-1. A micro-batch balance loss wants every row even: 2 tokens per expert in every sequence.
Global-batch balancing only asks the bottom row to be even. Code can lean on E1 and math on E2, while the batch as a whole stays at 8 per expert.

blocks.md: In their experiments (up to 42.8B total parameters and 400B tokens) the global-batch loss lowered pre-training perplexity by about 0.1 and raised benchmark scores by about 2 points, made experts visibly specialize by domain, and added under 3% latency in their setup. Their Figure 1 shows the same gap for aux-loss-free balancing: driving the bias from micro-batch counts did worse than from global-batch counts. The Qwen3 MoE models adopted the global-batch loss. It is the same batch-wise versus sequence-wise argument DeepSeek-V3 makes in lesson 6.

blocks.question: 4 experts, top-1, 8 tokens. Counts are (4, 2, 2, 0) and average router scores are P = (0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1). What is the sum of $f_i P_i$ (the loss divided by alpha)?
blocks.explain: $f_i = \frac{N}{KT} c_i = \frac{4}{8} c_i$, so f = (2, 1, 1, 0). Then 2(0.4) + 1(0.3) + 1(0.2) + 0(0.1) = 0.8 + 0.3 + 0.2 = 1.3, above the balanced value of 1.0. 0.325 is what you get if you forget the N/(KT) scaling and use raw fractions (0.5, 0.25, 0.25, 0).

blocks.question: Your MoE drops 4% of tokens at capacity factor 1.0. A teammate proposes raising the capacity factor to 2.0 and calling it fixed. What is the main cost?
options: None; capacity factor only affects inference
Each expert now reserves room for twice its fair share, so compute and memory are spent on padding while the underlying imbalance (and idle experts) remains
The auxiliary loss becomes undefined
Tokens are now routed to two experts each
blocks.explain: Capacity is a buffer per expert. Doubling it reduces drops but wastes compute and memory whenever experts are below capacity, which, under imbalance, is most of them. The Switch paper describes exactly this trade-off, and its Switch models performed better at low capacity factors (1.0 and 1.25).

blocks.question: An MoE is trained on 64 GPUs, each micro-batch holding 2 sequences, with the balance loss computed per micro-batch. Analysis shows every expert is used about equally on code, math and prose. Which change most directly allows domain specialization?
options: Raise alpha so the balance loss is stronger
Add a router z-loss
Synchronize the expert counts $f_i$ across all micro-batches and compute the balance loss on the global batch
Raise the capacity factor
blocks.explain: With 2 sequences per micro-batch, the loss forces each sequence to spread evenly, so code tokens cannot concentrate on code experts. Counting $f_i$ over the global batch only requires the corpus mix to be balanced. A larger alpha tightens the same wrong constraint; the z-loss is about logit size; capacity only changes dropping.

lessons.title: Aux-loss-free balancing: steer the router with a bias

blocks.md: **Loss-Free Balancing** (Wang, Gao, Zhao, Sun and Dai, DeepSeek-AI, 2024) controls load without any balance loss. Each expert gets a scalar **bias** $b_i$. The bias is added to the affinity scores only when choosing the top-K experts. The gate values that weight the experts' outputs still use the original scores.

blocks.tex: g_{i,t} = \begin{cases} s_{i,t} & s_{i,t} + b_i \in \mathrm{Topk}(\{s_{j,t} + b_j\}_{j=1}^{N},\ K) \\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}
blocks.caption: The bias decides who is selected; the unbiased score decides how much the selected expert contributes.

blocks.md: The biases are not learned by gradient descent. After each training step, count the tokens $c_i$ each expert received, compare with the mean $\bar c$, and move each bias by a fixed step $u$: up if the expert was underloaded, down if overloaded. Here $u$ is the paper's name for this update rate, not the hidden state $u_t$ of lesson 1. That is Algorithm 1 of the paper, with update rule $b_i \leftarrow b_i + u \cdot \mathrm{sign}(e_i)$, where the error is $e_i = \bar c - c_i$ (the paper's symbol, not the centroid $e_i$ of lesson 1) and sign gives +1 for a positive number, -1 for a negative one and 0 for zero. To score balance the paper defines **MaxVio** (maximal violation) = $(\max_i \text{Load}_i - \overline{\text{Load}}) / \overline{\text{Load}}$, how far the busiest expert is above a perfectly even share; 0 is perfect balance.

blocks.title: Algorithm 1 on the toy batch
blocks.code:
u = 0.05                    # bias update rate (paper: 0.001)
b = zeros(n_experts)        # one bias per expert, starts at 0
for batch in data:
    s = router_scores(batch)            # [T, n_experts]
    pick = topk(s + b, k=2)             # bias steers selection only
    g = gather(s, pick)                 # gates use the raw scores
    loss = lm_loss(batch, pick, g)      # no balance term
    loss.backward(); opt.step()         # b gets no gradient
    c = bincount(pick, n_experts)       # tokens per expert
    e = c.mean() - c                    # > 0 means underloaded
    b = b + u * sign(e)                 # nudge toward balance

scenes.caption: All biases start at 0, so the first step routes exactly like a plain top-K router.

vars.picks: A appears in all 8 tokens' top-2

scenes.caption: Selection uses s + b. The gate values come from s itself, so the forward computation is the model's honest opinion of each chosen expert.
The training loss is only the language-modeling loss. Nothing in it mentions balance, so no interference gradient reaches the router.
After the step, count each expert's tokens. A and B are over the mean of 4; C and D are under.
Each bias moves by exactly u in the direction of its error's sign. The size of the error does not matter in this rule.
Step 1: B is now under the mean, so its bias swings back up to 0 while A keeps sinking.

blocks.title: Expert loads per step in the toy (8 tokens, top-2, u = 0.05)

scenes.caption: Step 0, all biases 0: routing follows raw scores. Expert A takes all 8 tokens, D gets 1. Mean load is 4 (8 tokens x top-2 / 4 experts). MaxVio = (8 - 4) / 4 = 1.0.
Biases after one update: A and B were above 4, so they drop by u = 0.05; C and D rise. Loads become (8, 3, 3, 2): B lost slots, A has not moved yet.
Step 2, bias (-0.10, 0, +0.10, +0.10): loads (7, 4, 3, 2), MaxVio 0.75. Overloaded experts keep sinking, underloaded ones keep rising.
Step 3, bias (-0.15, 0, +0.15, +0.15). A is down to 6. B's bias stalled at 0 because its load was exactly 4 last step: sign(0) = 0.
Step 4, bias (-0.20, +0.05, +0.15, +0.20): loads (6, 3, 4, 3), MaxVio 0.5. Overloaded experts keep sinking, underloaded ones keep rising.
Step 5, bias (-0.25, +0.10, +0.15, +0.25): loads (5, 4, 3, 4), MaxVio 0.25. No gradient was ever involved; only the four bias numbers moved.
Step 6, bias (-0.30, +0.10, +0.20, +0.25): loads (4, 3, 4, 5), MaxVio 0.25. Overloaded experts keep sinking, underloaded ones keep rising.
From here the toy oscillates between (4, 3, 4, 5) and (4, 5, 4, 3): 16 slots over 8 tokens are too coarse to hit 4 each every step. Real batches have millions of slots, and u is 0.001.

blocks.md: Simplified: in this toy the router scores are frozen, so only the bias moves. In real training the router weights also change each step, and the bias keeps tracking the load. The 8 token-by-4 expert scores and every load and bias shown were computed by a script.

Look at one token at step 6, bias $(-0.30, +0.10, +0.20, +0.25)$. Its raw scores are $(0.80, 0.70, 0.20, 0.35)$, so a plain router would pick A and B. Biased scores are $(0.50, 0.80, 0.40, 0.60)$, so it picks **B and D** instead. Its gates use the raw 0.70 and 0.35; normalized over the chosen pair as DeepSeek-V3 does, that is $0.67$ and $0.33$.

blocks.prompt: The toy used u = 0.05. Predict what happens with u = 0.1 (bigger steps).
blocks.reveal: It gets near balance faster (MaxVio 0.25 at step 3) but then overshoots: at step 4 loads jump to (2, 7, 4, 3), MaxVio 0.75, and it keeps swinging. The paper saw the same effect at scale: u = 0.0001 converged too slowly early in training, u = 0.01 caused fluctuations late in training, and u = 0.001 was best (validation perplexity 9.50 vs 9.51 for both others).

blocks.md: The bias changes **which** experts a token uses, never **how much** a chosen expert contributes, and it receives no gradient. That is how Loss-Free Balancing controls load without fighting the language-modeling objective.

Why update from the **previous** batch instead of balancing the current one exactly? Because using the current sequence's load would let later tokens influence earlier tokens' routing, leaking information about the future in a causal language model. **Expert Choice** routing, where each expert picks its top tokens, balances perfectly but has exactly this leak. The paper bounds it by counting (Appendix D.1): in a chunk of $T$ tokens each of the $N$ experts picks $KT/N$ of them, so there are $\binom{T}{KT/N}^N$ possible assignments, and log2 of that count per token is how many bits the assignment can carry. It shows this exceeds $K \log_2((1-R)/R)$ per layer, with $R = K/N$. For $K = 2$, $N = 16$: $2 \log_2 7 \approx 5.6$ bits, about 50 over 9 layers. It also saw an abnormal 10% loss drop when it made leakage easier.

**Results** (1B model on 100B tokens, 3B on 200B tokens, sigmoid gating, DeepSeekMoE backbone). Sigmoid gating scores each expert on its own as $\sigma(u_t^\top e_i)$ instead of a softmax across experts; the paper found it worked better. Balance is measured with MaxVio, defined above, on validation data. Against an auxiliary loss with $\alpha$ = 0.001:

blocks.title: Loss-controlled vs Loss-Free (Wang et al., Table 2)

scenes.caption: Global MaxVio on validation data, averaged over layers: the busiest expert was 72% (1B) and 52% (3B) over its fair share with the aux loss, but only 4% with Loss-Free Balancing.
Validation perplexity at the same time: 9.56 vs 9.50 at 1B and 7.97 vs 7.92 at 3B. Better balance and slightly better quality, no trade-off.

blocks.question: A colleague's implementation computes `weights = gather(s + b, pick)` and multiplies expert outputs by those weights. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; using the biased score everywhere is the method
The top-K must be taken on s alone, and the bias added after
The bias should be multiplied, not added
The bias now changes each expert's contribution to the output, so a balancing knob leaks into the model's function; gates must use the raw scores s
blocks.explain: The paper and DeepSeek-V3 both state that the bias is only used for routing; the gate value comes from the original affinity. With the bug, an underloaded expert's output is inflated just because it was underloaded, which distorts the forward pass. (A multiplicative bias was tested and was slightly worse, but it too only affects selection.)

blocks.question: Why does Algorithm 1 use sign(e) rather than e itself?
options: The paper tried b += u x e and found it slightly better balanced but no better in perplexity, so it kept the simpler sign rule
sign(e) is required for causality
Using e would make the bias receive gradients
sign(e) guarantees exact balance every step
blocks.explain: Table 3 of the paper compares variants: the proportional rule reached MaxVio 0.028 to 0.040 with perplexity 9.51 to 9.53, versus 0.044 and 9.50 for the sign rule with u = 0.001. Neither variant involves gradients or future tokens.

lessons.title: Putting it together: routing in DeepSeek-V3

blocks.md: DeepSeek-V3 (671B total, 37B activated) uses all three ideas. Each of its 58 MoE layers has 1 shared and 256 routed experts, picks 8 routed experts per token, and balances them with the bias method. Two details differ from DeepSeekMoE: affinities use a **sigmoid** per expert (a 0 to 1 score computed for each expert on its own) instead of a softmax across experts, and the chosen experts' scores are **normalized** to sum to 1 to give the gates. The released code then multiplies the normalized gates by a constant `route_scale` (2.5 in config_671B.json). Normalized gates always sum to 1, so this fixed factor sets how large the routed experts' combined output is next to the shared expert and the residual; the report does not explain the chosen value.

blocks.tex: s_{i,t} = \sigma(u_t^\top e_i),\qquad g'_{i,t} = \begin{cases} s_{i,t} & s_{i,t} + b_i \in \mathrm{Topk}(\{s_{j,t} + b_j\}, K_r) \\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases},\qquad g_{i,t} = \frac{g'_{i,t}}{\sum_j g'_{j,t}}
blocks.caption: DeepSeek-V3 routing (Eqs. 13 to 16 of the report, with the bias), $K_r = 8$. In words: score each expert with a sigmoid, keep the raw scores of the 8 experts with the highest biased scores, and divide each kept score by their sum so the gates add to 1.

blocks.md: There is also a hardware constraint. Experts are spread over 64 GPUs in 8 **nodes** (servers of 8 GPUs each). GPUs inside a node talk over **NVLink**, NVIDIA's direct GPU-to-GPU link (160 GB/s); nodes talk over **InfiniBand**, a datacenter network (50 GB/s). Crossing nodes is about 160 / 50 = 3.2 times slower, so V3 uses **node-limited routing**: each token may go to at most $M = 4$ nodes, chosen by the sum of the highest $K_r/M$ (here 8 / 4 = 2) affinity scores of the experts on each node. The released inference code expresses the same idea as **group-limited** routing: 8 expert groups (`n_expert_groups`), keep the best 4 (`n_limited_groups`), scoring each group by the sum of its top-2 biased scores.

blocks.title: Group-limited gate on a toy token (8 experts, 4 groups)
blocks.code:
def gate(x, W, bias, n_groups=4, keep_groups=2, k=3, scale=2.5):
    s = sigmoid(x @ W.T)                     # affinity per expert
    biased = s + bias                        # bias only steers selection
    g = biased.view(n_groups, -1)            # 8 experts -> 4 groups of 2
    group_score = g.topk(2).values.sum(-1)   # sum of top-2 per group
    keep = group_score.topk(keep_groups).indices
    mask = ones(n_groups, dtype=bool); mask[keep] = False
    g = g.masked_fill(mask[:, None], -inf).flatten()
    idx = g.topk(k).indices                  # chosen experts
    w = s[idx]                               # raw scores, not biased
    w = w / w.sum()                          # normalize (sigmoid case)
    return w * scale, idx

scenes.caption: Sigmoid affinities for one token. Raw ranking: expert 5 (0.818), expert 0 (0.769), expert 3 (0.711). Simplified from DeepSeek-V3's inference/model.py Gate.forward, shrunk to 8 experts.
The load-balancing biases (set by the update rule, not by gradients) are added. Expert 5 has been overloaded (bias -0.15) and expert 4 underloaded (+0.20).
Experts are grouped in pairs; each group's score is the sum of its 2 best biased scores. Group 1 (experts 2, 3) leads.
Only the top 2 groups survive. Expert 0, the second-best raw score, is cut because its group lost. This is the price of capping communication.
Top-3 among eligible biased scores: experts 3 (0.761), 7 (0.690), 6 (0.575). Without groups the choice would have been 3, 0, 7.

Gates come from the unbiased scores, normalized to sum to 1, then multiplied by route_scale, a config constant (2.5 in config_671B.json) that sets the routed experts' weight next to the shared expert and residual.

blocks.title: Node-limited dispatch (simplified: 4 nodes, M = 2)

scenes.caption: A token's chosen experts may sit on many nodes. Each cross-node hop uses slow InfiniBand, so the router first ranks nodes.
Nodes are scored from their experts' best affinities; only the top M survive (V3 uses M = 4 of 8 nodes). Experts on nodes B and D are now ineligible for this token.
The token crosses InfiniBand once per kept node, landing on the GPU with the same in-node index, then NVLink forwards it to the GPUs that host its experts.

blocks.md: Training settings from the report: bias update speed $\gamma = 0.001$ (the update rate the loss-free paper calls $u$) for the first 14.3T tokens, then $\gamma = 0$ (biases frozen) for the last 500B. A **complementary sequence-wise balance loss** (the same $\alpha \sum f_i P_i$ form, but with $f_i$ and $P_i$ computed over the tokens of one sequence instead of the whole batch) with a tiny $\alpha = 0.0001$ guards against extreme imbalance inside any single sequence. Thanks to good balance, V3 drops no tokens in training; deployment strategies such as redundant experts (extra copies of busy experts, described below) keep inference drop-free too.

Why mostly batch-wise balancing? A sequence-wise loss forces each sequence to spread over all experts, even a sequence that is entirely code. Batch-wise balancing only asks the whole batch to be even, so experts can specialize by domain. The report shows clearer domain-specific expert load in an aux-loss-free 16B model, and at 1B scale validation loss was 2.258 with a sequence-wise loss vs 2.253 for both the loss-free method and a batch-wise aux loss (3B: 2.085 vs 2.080 and 2.080).

The figure scores five standard benchmarks, each as the percentage of problems solved: **HumanEval** (164 Python programming tasks from OpenAI, checked by unit tests, solved on the first attempt), **GSM8K** (grade-school math word problems), **MATH** (12,500 competition math problems), **BBH** (BIG-Bench Hard, 23 hard reasoning tasks) and **MMLU** (multiple-choice questions across 57 subjects).

blocks.title: Aux-loss-based vs aux-loss-free at 228.7B total (DeepSeek-V3 Table 5)

scenes.caption: Baseline balanced purely with auxiliary losses (20.9B activated, 578B training tokens).
Same data and architecture, auxiliary losses removed, bias balancing added. Most benchmarks improve (HumanEval 46.3, GSM8K 74.5); MMLU slipped from 68.3 to 67.2. Gains are typical, not universal.

blocks.md: Serving adds its own balancing. Load observed online decides which experts are hot; V3 duplicates high-load experts (**redundant experts**), re-chosen periodically such as every 10 minutes, with 32 redundant experts in the **prefill** deployment (the stage that processes the whole prompt at once). In **decoding** (generating output one token at a time), the shared expert is treated as a routed expert that is always selected, so each token picks 9 experts, with 64 GPUs hosting redundant and shared experts.

Batch-level balance has two weak spots the report names: imbalance inside a single sequence or small batch, and **domain shift** at inference (a deployment flooded with one kind of input overloads that domain's experts). V3 answers the first with large training batches plus the tiny sequence-wise loss, and the second with redundant experts at serving time.

blocks.question: In the gate trace, expert 0 had the second-highest raw affinity (0.769) but was not chosen. Why?
options: Its bias was negative enough to drop it below experts 6 and 7
Sigmoid scores above 0.75 are clipped
Its group (experts 0 and 1) had a lower group score than groups 1 and 3, so the whole group was masked before the top-k
Shared experts always take the place of expert 0
blocks.explain: Group 0 scored 0.719 + 0.501 = 1.220, behind groups 1 (1.335) and 3 (1.265). Masking happens before the expert-level top-k, so expert 0's biased 0.719, which would beat expert 7's 0.690, never competes. That is the deliberate cost of limiting how many nodes a token touches.

blocks.question: DeepSeek-V3 relies on the bias method yet still keeps a sequence-wise balance loss with alpha = 0.0001. What is the best justification?
options: The bias method does not work without an auxiliary loss
The bias balances load across whole batches; the tiny loss only guards against extreme imbalance within a single sequence, while staying too weak to cause meaningful interference gradients
The loss replaces the bias during the final 500B tokens
It is needed to train the router weights at all
blocks.explain: The report calls it complementary: the main balancing is aux-loss-free, and the sequence-wise term exists just to avoid extreme per-sequence imbalance. Its alpha is ten times smaller than the 0.001 baseline used in the loss-free paper. Router weights are trained by the language-modeling loss through the gate values.

blocks.question: A team copies V3's recipe but trains with very small global batches (a few sequences per step). Which risk grows most?
options: Future-token leakage from the bias
The shared expert stops training
Node-limited routing stops working
Per-step load imbalance, since batch-wise balancing cannot even out a batch that is mostly one domain, so busy experts stall the step
blocks.explain: The loss-free paper shows balance improving as the computation batch grows, and the V3 report lists imbalance within small batches as a challenge that large-scale expert and data parallelism (model copies each training on a different slice of the batch) solves. The bias uses only past batches, so there is no leakage.

lessons.title: Build it: a DeepSeekMoE layer with bias balancing in your GPT

blocks.md: Time to turn the equations into tensor code. You will replace the MLP in each block of the GPT you built with a DeepSeek-style MoE layer: 16 small SwiGLU experts, a sigmoid router with top-2 selection and normalized gates (as in V3), one shared expert, and a bias for balancing. The hard part is not the math but the bookkeeping. A batch arrives as one tensor of tokens, yet token 0 must visit experts 2 and 0 while token 1 visits experts 1 and 2. Every real implementation solves this with the same four moves: route, sort by expert, run each expert on its slice, scatter the results back.

blocks.code:
import torch, torch.nn as nn
from torch.nn import functional as F

class SwiGLU(nn.Module):                      # one expert: w2(silu(x w1) * (x w3))
    def __init__(self, d, h):
        super().__init__()
        self.w1 = nn.Linear(d, h, bias=False)
        self.w3 = nn.Linear(d, h, bias=False)
        self.w2 = nn.Linear(h, d, bias=False)
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.w2(F.silu(self.w1(x)) * self.w3(x))

class MoE(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, n_exp=16, k=2, h=128, n_shared=1):
        super().__init__()
        self.n_exp, self.k = n_exp, k
        # routed experts as stacked tensors: expert e uses w1[e], w3[e], w2[e]
        self.w1 = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(n_exp, d, h) * 0.02)
        self.w3 = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(n_exp, d, h) * 0.02)
        self.w2 = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(n_exp, h, d) * 0.02)
        self.centroids = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(n_exp, d) * 0.02)  # e_i
        self.register_buffer('bias', torch.zeros(n_exp))  # b_i: no gradient
        self.shared = SwiGLU(d, n_shared * h) if n_shared else None
        self.counts = torch.zeros(n_exp)    # tokens per expert, last step
        self.aux = torch.tensor(0.0)        # balance loss, last step
blocks.caption: moe.py, part 1: experts stored as stacked weight tensors, the router's centroids, and a bias buffer.

blocks.md: Storing the routed experts as three stacked tensors (`w1[e]`, `w3[e]`, `w2[e]` for expert `e`) instead of 16 separate modules keeps all expert weights in a few contiguous blocks, the layout grouped kernels expect. The bias is a **buffer** (`register_buffer`): it is saved with the model and moves to the GPU with it, but it is not a parameter, so the optimizer never touches it and it receives no gradient. `F.silu` is PyTorch's name for the Swish function of lesson 3. Each expert has hidden width `h`; the shared expert is one SwiGLU of width `n_shared * h`, the same as DeepSeek-V3's `MLP(dim, n_shared_experts * moe_inter_dim)`.

blocks.code:
def forward(self, x):
        B, T, C = x.shape
        u = x.reshape(-1, C)                            # [N, C] tokens
        s = torch.sigmoid(u @ self.centroids.T)         # [N, E] affinities
        idx = torch.topk(s + self.bias, self.k, dim=-1).indices  # select
        g = s.gather(1, idx)                            # gates: raw scores
        g = g / g.sum(-1, keepdim=True)                 # normalize
blocks.caption: moe.py, part 2: route. Selection uses s + bias; the gates use the raw scores s, then normalize.

blocks.title: Dispatch on a toy batch: 4 tokens, top-2, 4 experts

scenes.caption: Top-2 picks: token 0 chose (2, 0), token 1 (1, 2), token 2 (0, 2), token 3 (3, 1). Flattened, row r belongs to token r // 2.
argsort by expert id (stable) gives order (1, 4, 2, 7, 0, 3, 5, 6). Reordered, the rows for each expert are contiguous, and tok = order // 2 remembers where each came from.
bincount gives the slice sizes (2, 2, 3, 1): expert 0 runs on rows 0 to 1, expert 1 on 2 to 3, expert 2 on 4 to 6, expert 3 on row 7. Each is one dense matrix multiply.
Combine: each output row is scaled by its gate and index_add_ sums it into its source token. Token 2 receives rows 1 and 6, from experts 0 and 2.

blocks.code:
# dispatch: one row per (token, slot), sorted by expert id
        flat = idx.flatten()                            # [N*k]
        order = torch.argsort(flat, stable=True)
        tok = order // self.k                           # source token of row
        counts = torch.bincount(flat, minlength=self.n_exp)
        xs = u[tok]                                     # gathered inputs
        out = torch.empty_like(xs)
        start = 0
        for e, n in enumerate(counts.tolist()):         # contiguous slices
            if n == 0:
                continue
            h = xs[start:start + n]
            out[start:start + n] = (F.silu(h @ self.w1[e]) * (h @ self.w3[e])) @ self.w2[e]
            start += n
        # combine: scale by gate, scatter-add back to each source token
        y = torch.zeros_like(u).index_add_(0, tok, out * g.flatten()[order, None])
        if self.shared is not None:
            y = y + self.shared(u)                      # always-on expert
        # bookkeeping for balancing (aux loss uses normalized scores)
        self.counts = counts.detach()
        f = counts.float() * self.n_exp / (self.k * u.shape[0])
        P = (s / s.sum(-1, keepdim=True)).mean(0)
        self.aux = (f * P).sum()
        return y.view(B, T, C)
blocks.caption: moe.py, part 3: dispatch with argsort and bincount, run each expert on its slice, combine with index_add_.

blocks.md: Three details matter. `index_add_` *adds* rows that share a destination; with top-2 every token appears twice in `tok`, so plain indexed assignment would keep only one of its experts. The gates are reordered with the same `order` as the rows, so each output is scaled by its own token's gate. And the Python loop over experts is the simple version: DeepSeek-V3's released inference code does the same per expert with `torch.where(indices == i)`, while fast training kernels run all slices in one grouped matrix multiply (lesson 8).

blocks.caption: moe.py, part 4, and where it sits in train.py. The bias moves after opt.step(), outside autograd.

blocks.md: Order of operations: forward (selection uses the current bias, counts are recorded), backward and optimizer step (the bias is not involved), then `update_bias` from those same counts. In V3 terms, the update rate is $\gamma = 0.001$; MaxVio is logged from the same counts. If your loop uses gradient accumulation, sum the counts over all micro-steps before updating, or the bias sees only the last micro-batch (lesson 4's global-batch point).

blocks.md: How to read this honestly. The balance result is clear and repeated across both seeds: with no balancing the router settles into a lopsided state, and both methods fix it, the bias method ending more balanced without adding any term to the loss. The quality result is not: at this scale the validation losses differ by less than the seed-to-seed noise, so the lab cannot confirm or refute the small perplexity gains the loss-free paper measured at 1B and 3B parameters. What imbalance costs here is invisible, because one CPU runs every expert anyway; it becomes real once experts sit on different GPUs (lesson 8).

Do not read quality conclusions off a run this small. Character-level Shakespeare with a 3.65M-parameter MoE (0.9M active) trains in under an hour per run on a CPU; differences of a few thousandths in validation loss between configurations are within seed noise. What this lab shows reliably is the mechanism: what the router does without balancing, and how each method changes the expert loads.

blocks.question: A teammate replaces the combine line with `y = torch.zeros_like(u); y[tok] = out * g.flatten()[order, None]`. Tests with K = 1 pass. What goes wrong with K = 2?
options: Nothing; indexed assignment and index_add_ are the same
Every token index appears twice in `tok`, and assignment keeps only one write per index, so each token silently gets only one of its two experts
The gradients to the gates become zero
The shapes no longer match, so it raises an error
blocks.explain: With top-2, `tok` lists each token twice. `index_add_` sums both expert outputs into the token's row; indexed assignment overwrites, so only one survives, with no error. With K = 1 each token appears once, so the bug hides. So pair the dense-equivalence test with a K = 2 check against a slow per-token loop; test_moe.py above lacks one.

blocks.question: Where must `update_bias` run relative to the training step?
options: Before the forward pass, using the counts the forward pass will produce
Inside the loss, so autograd can adjust it
After `opt.step()`, under `torch.no_grad()`, using the counts recorded by this step's forward pass, and before an evaluation pass overwrites them
Only at the end of training, once
blocks.explain: Algorithm 1 adjusts the bias from the load just observed, outside the gradient computation. Running it inside autograd would make it a learned parameter (and leak balance into the loss), and running it after an eval forward would balance the wrong batch. Counts from the current step only steer the next step's routing, so no future token leaks.

lessons.title: MoE on real hardware: expert parallelism, all-to-all and serving

blocks.md: Your MoE layer ran on one device, so every expert sat in the same memory. DeepSeek-V3 cannot do that. Its 671B parameters stored in FP8 (one byte each, the format of the released weights) take about 671 GB, while one server of eight 80 GB GPUs holds 640 GB in total, before any activations or cache. So the experts are spread over many GPUs: **expert parallelism** (EP), the scheme GShard used to shard a Transformer's experts across devices. Each GPU stores only its own experts, and tokens travel to the experts that their router picked.

blocks.title: One MoE layer under expert parallelism, 3 GPUs

scenes.caption: Each GPU holds a slice of the batch and two experts. After routing, GPU 0 sends each token's hidden vector to the GPUs that own its chosen experts.
Every GPU does the same at once: an all-to-all exchange, where each GPU sends a different piece to every other. This is the dispatch.
Each GPU now runs its local experts on whatever arrived: one contiguous slice per expert, as in the lesson 7 code.
The combine is a second all-to-all in the opposite direction: expert outputs go home, where they are scaled by the gates and summed per token.

blocks.md: So every MoE layer becomes four steps: route, **dispatch** (all-to-all), local expert compute, **combine** (all-to-all). V3's report sizes the traffic. A token's hidden vector is 7168 numbers; V3 quantizes it to FP8 before the dispatch (plus small scale factors) and keeps the combine in BF16 for precision. With node-limited routing (lesson 6) a token crosses InfiniBand to at most 4 nodes, one copy per node, and is then forwarded over NVLink to the GPUs holding its experts. That caps the InfiniBand dispatch at about $4 \times 7168 = 28{,}672$ bytes per token per layer, instead of up to twice that if all 8 experts sat on different nodes.

The report calls the resulting **computation-to-communication ratio** about 1:1: an MoE layer spends roughly as long moving tokens as computing on them. Its answer is to overlap the two. Its pipeline schedule, **DualPipe**, splits each chunk of work into attention, all-to-all dispatch, MLP and all-to-all combine, and interleaves a forward chunk with a backward chunk so one's communication runs while the other computes, with only 20 of the GPU's streaming multiprocessors (its compute units) dedicated to communication. DeepSeek later open-sourced its dispatch and combine kernels as **DeepEP**. In serving, the same idea appears as two micro-batches, one computing while the other communicates.

blocks.title: Two micro-batches through one MoE layer, without and with overlap

scenes.caption: Simplified model with stage times we chose (attention 4, dispatch 3, MLP 4, combine 3 time units), compute and communication about 1:1. Run in order, micro-batches A and B take 28 units and each lane sits idle roughly half the time.
Overlapped: while A's tokens are in flight, the GPU computes B's attention, and so on. The same work finishes at 19 units. Real schedules (DualPipe) also interleave forward and backward chunks.

blocks.md: Now the arithmetic behind lesson 2's warning that small experts run less efficiently. With $B$ tokens in a step, 256 routed experts and top-8, there are $8B$ expert slots, so an expert receives on average $8B/256 = B/32$ tokens. Its up-projection is one matrix multiply (a **GEMM**, general matrix multiply) of a $(B/32) \times 7168$ matrix by a $7168 \times 2048$ weight. The **arithmetic intensity** of a matrix multiply is its FLOPs divided by the bytes it moves from memory; when it is below the GPU's FLOPs-to-bandwidth ratio (its **ridge point**), the kernel waits on memory instead of computing. For an $m \times k$ by $k \times n$ product in 16-bit numbers:

blocks.tex: I = \frac{2mkn\ \text{FLOPs}}{2(kn + mk + mn)\ \text{bytes}} \approx m \quad \text{when}\ m \ll k, n
blocks.caption: Weights ($kn$) dominate the bytes when few rows arrive, so intensity is roughly the number of tokens the expert got.

blocks.title: Arithmetic intensity of one V3 expert GEMM vs the dense FFN

scenes.caption: Ridge 295 FLOPs per byte: an H100 SXM's (NVIDIA's Hopper data-center GPU, server-module form) dense BF16 peak (about 989 TFLOP/s) over its 3.35 TB/s memory bandwidth. Below the line, a kernel is limited by memory, not math.
At B = 4096 tokens a V3 expert gets 128 rows: intensity 118, still memory-bound. V3's dense FFN (width 18432, all B rows) is at 2284. Fine-grained experts need about 32 times more tokens per step.
Decode with B = 64 tokens: 2 rows per expert, intensity 2, two orders of magnitude below the ridge. Move the slider: no realistic GPU puts this anywhere near compute-bound.

blocks.md: Two older ways to cope with uneven expert loads. Switch-style **capacity** (lesson 4) gives every expert a fixed-size buffer, which keeps shapes static but forces a choice between dropping tokens and padding. **MegaBlocks** (Gale et al., 2022) instead writes the expert computation as **block-sparse** matrix multiplies: the tokens of all experts are packed together and each expert's block can have any number of rows, so nothing is dropped or padded (a **dropless MoE**). It reported end-to-end training speedups of up to 40% over Tutel, Microsoft's MoE training library. OLMoE uses dropless routing, and V3 drops no tokens in training thanks to its balance. Kernels that run all experts' variable-sized multiplies in one launch are usually called **grouped GEMMs**.

Serving turns the picture around. All 671B parameters must be resident although a token uses 37B, and in decoding (one new token per sequence per step) the batch is small, so each step is limited by reading weights from memory. The report says it directly: in decode, the batch per expert is usually within 256 tokens and the bottleneck is memory access rather than computation. Batching helps less than for a dense model, because more tokens also touch more distinct experts, so more weights must be read. In a simplified model where each token picks 8 of 256 experts uniformly at random, a layer touches $256(1 - (1 - 8/256)^B)$ distinct experts in a step of $B$ tokens:

blocks.title: Distinct experts whose weights a decode step must read (per layer)

scenes.caption: One token reads 8 experts' weights. By 32 tokens, about 163 of 256 experts are touched, so the step reads most of the layer for only 32 tokens of output. Simplified: real routing is skewed, not uniform.
Past about 128 tokens almost every expert is touched, so the weight bytes per step stop growing and each extra token is nearly free. Large decode batches are how MoE serving becomes efficient.

blocks.md: That is why V3 is served across many GPUs with large aggregate batches. The report's decode unit is 40 nodes (320 GPUs) with each GPU hosting one expert and 64 GPUs hosting redundant and shared experts (lesson 6); DeepSeek's February 2025 serving overview describes 18-node decode units with 2 routed experts per GPU. That overview also gives measured production throughput on H800 nodes (8 GPUs each; the H800 is the H100 variant DeepSeek uses): about 73.7k input tokens per second per node in prefill (counting prompt tokens served from its cache) and about 14.8k output tokens per second per node in decode. These are DeepSeek's measurements, not run here, and deployments change over time.

MoE cost is not just FLOPs. Every layer adds two all-to-alls that must be overlapped with compute, small experts need many tokens per step to stop being memory-bound, and serving must keep all experts resident and batch widely enough that reading their weights is shared by many tokens.

blocks.question: A team switches from 64 experts with top-2 to 256 experts with top-8, each a quarter as wide, keeping active parameters fixed. A step routes 2048 tokens. How many rows does each expert's GEMM get on average, and what changes?
options: 16 rows after the switch, because 4 times as many experts share the tokens
256 rows after the switch, because top-8 sends 4 times as many copies of each token
Nothing changes, because FLOPs per token are equal
64 rows in both designs (2048 x 2 / 64 and 2048 x 8 / 256), so intensity stays near 60, but there are 4 times as many GEMMs, each a quarter the size, and each token goes to 4 times as many experts
blocks.explain: Tokens per expert = B x K / N, and K and N both grew 4 times. Rows per expert stay at 64, so each GEMM is still memory-bound at the same intensity, but the same work is now split over 4 times as many smaller launches and dispatch destinations. Fine granularity costs efficiency unless kernels group the experts and batches grow.

blocks.question: A single-user chat with DeepSeek-V3 generates one token at a time (batch 1). Which resource sets the speed of each MoE layer?
options: Tensor core FLOPs, because 37B active parameters is a lot of math
Memory bandwidth: the step must read the 8 chosen experts' weights (plus the shared expert) for a single token, at an arithmetic intensity of about 1
InfiniBand bandwidth only, because experts are on other nodes
The router's top-k, since it is sequential
blocks.explain: With one token, each expert GEMM has one row, so intensity is about 1 FLOP per byte, far below any GPU's ridge. The layer's time is the time to read those weights (plus communication if experts are remote). This is why providers batch many users together, as the experts-touched curve shows.
